title: Three-letter roots
hook: most Hebrew words grow from a root of three letters

segments.voice: Yesterday, baruch atah: blessed are you, the opening of a blessing. Your line was baruch atah. What did you pause over? Today the alphabet is behind us, and we go underground, to the roots. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

A student, a teacher, the Talmud, and an hour of study. Four things that seem to have nothing in common. One sits at a desk. One stands at the front. One fills a long shelf of heavy volumes. One is the time you set aside to open a book. But say them in Hebrew and listen: talmid, melamed, Talmud, limud. The same three sounds keep surfacing, l, m, d, like the same family face showing up in a row of old photographs. That's not a coincidence. It's how Hebrew is built: three letters underneath, and a whole family of words growing out of them.
screen: `A STUDENT, A TEACHER, A SHELF, A STUDY.` → `TALMID, MELAMED, TALMUD, LIMUD.` → `THE SAME FAMILY FACE.`

segments.voice: Shoresh. A root. Turn it four ways. First, the idea. A great many Hebrew words grow from a root of three consonants. The root carries a core meaning. Vowels, and letters added before, after or between, turn it into a noun, a verb, a person, a place. Second, a root you've already met. Lamed, mem, dalet carries learning. Lamad: he learned. Talmid: a student, one who learns. Melamed: a teacher, one who makes others learn. Talmud: the great body of study. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people to hear the laws "that ye may learn them," and in Hebrew, the word for learn is built on those same three letters. Third, a second root. Kaf, tav, vet carries writing. Katav: he wrote. Michtav: a letter you'd mail. Ktav: handwriting. And Ketuvim, the Writings, the third part of the Hebrew Bible, the Psalms and Proverbs and Ruth. Fourth, the picture in the word itself. Shoresh is the root of a tree. In Jeremiah, the one who trusts in God is like a tree planted by water, sending its roots out toward the stream. You see the branches, the leaves, the fruit. The root stays under the ground, holding it all together. For the next stretch of the path, we'll dig up one root a day, and watch what grows out of it.
screen: `THREE CONSONANTS, ONE CORE MEANING.` · `L-M-D: LEARN, STUDENT, TEACHER.` · `K-T-V: WROTE, LETTER, WRITINGS.` · `A TREE'S ROOTS BY THE WATER.` · then, large: `THREE-LETTER ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one root. Settle, and breathe. Say these slowly, and listen for the three sounds that stay: lamad, talmid, melamed, Talmud. L, m, d. Now try the other: katav, michtav, Ketuvim. K, t, v. Then let the words fall away and keep only the three letters, the way the root stays in the ground while the leaves come and go. Sit with that for a few breaths: what stays, under everything that changes. If you pray, you can do the same with a word from a prayer you know. The bell holds the time.
Shoresh. A root: the three letters underneath a family of Hebrew words, and the root of a tree. Today's word.
Your line: three-letter roots. Today, find one Hebrew word you already know, and ask what its three letters might be. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Students of Hebrew learn to find the three-letter root of a word, and dictionaries of biblical Hebrew are often arranged by root rather than by spelling.

pairs: the Writings, part of the Hebrew Bible

shoresh only means a word's root, never a plant's

fork.setup: you hear katav, michtav and Ketuvim. what do they share?
fork.reveal: the root kaf, tav, vet: he wrote, a letter, the Writings.

original.note: Hebrew: a root, of a tree or of a word.

trapdoor: what you thought: every Hebrew word has to be memorized on its own.
what it means: a great many grow from three consonants, so one root opens a whole family of words.
what a scholar hears: Ketuvim, the name of the third part of the Hebrew Bible, comes from k-t-v, the root of writing.

notes: Index hook says 'most Hebrew words'; the script says 'a great many' to keep within the claims rule. Confirm.
Deuteronomy 5:1 fragment quoted as JPS 1917 (KJV has the same words); u-lemadtem from L-M-D. Confirm.
Jeremiah 17:8 paraphrased (tree planted by water, spreading roots by the stream); the word there is shorashav. Confirm.
Roots L-M-D (lamad, talmid, melamed, Talmud) and K-T-V (katav, michtav, ktav, Ketuvim) are standard lexicon entries; confirm. Melamed glossed as teacher.
